name: Body hacking

card.summary: Applying a hacker ethic to one's own body, from tracking biomarkers and nootropics to DIY implants and self-administered compounds, in order to enhance function, energy and appearance.
card.note: Ranges from low-risk tracking to unregulated injectables and DIY implants with documented complications.

quick.overview:
Body hacking (also biohacking or grinder culture) means experimenting on your own body with the mindset of a software hacker: measure, tweak, repeat. It spans quantified-self tracking, nutrition and supplements, nootropics, wearable devices, DIY implants such as RFID chips and magnets, and self-administered drugs and peptides.

In looksmaxxing circles the appeal is using self-experimentation to improve energy, recovery, body composition and appearance. Medical literature describes a wide range of practices with very different risk levels, and reviews of unregulated injectables and chip implants document complications and limited safety data.
quick.how: Practitioners usually start with data, such as sleep, bloodwork and wearable metrics, and then change one variable at a time: diet, supplements, light exposure, training, or devices. A subset moves to implants or unapproved compounds, often obtained outside medical supervision. Results are tracked by the individual and shared in forums.
quick.risks: Risks scale with the practice. Hand surgeons report infection and tendon attrition from chip implants, and reviews of unregulated peptides cite contamination, inaccurate dosing and unknown long-term safety. A 2019 Lancet paper links biohacking and macronutrient fixation to eating-disorder trends in adolescent boys.

lead: Body hacking is the application of the hacker ethic, often with high risk tolerance, to enhance or change the body's functions, using technology such as do-it-yourself cybernetic devices or biochemicals [1]. A related sense, biohacking, means managing one's own biology through medical, nutritional and electronic methods such as nootropics and biometric tracking [2]. A 2018 review describes it as do-it-yourself citizen science that merges body modification with technology, motivated by cybernetic exploration, personal data and open-source medicine [3].

In looksmaxxing and fitness communities the term is used for self-experimentation aimed at energy, sleep, body composition, recovery and appearance, from tracking and supplements to unapproved injectable peptides [4]. Medical journals have also examined the implant branch of the culture, such as RFID chips in the hand [5], and the DIY brain stimulation wing [6].

chain: Adjust diet, supplements, devices or compounds
Better recovery, energy and physique that the person believes improve how they look
angle.text: Practitioners self-experiment with nutrition, tracking and sometimes compounds in the hope of improving recovery, body composition and energy, which they link to looking better. Implant-style body hacking is mostly about function rather than looks.

infobox: Biohacking, grinder culture, quantified self, DIY biology

paras: Wikipedia describes body hacking as the hacker ethic applied to the body, with biohacking as a broader label that includes nutrition, nootropics and biometrics [1][2]. Related strands include DIY biology, quantified self, synthetic biology and performance psychology [2].

Wikipedia dates the intellectual roots to Manfred Clynes and Nathan Kline's 1960 paper on cyborgs, Donna Haraway's 1985 Cyborg Manifesto and Kevin Warwick's 1998 chip implant. Amal Graafstra implanted an RFID chip in 2005 and founded Dangerous Things in 2013, and media covered the grinder movement in 2012 [1]. Groups such as Grindhouse Wetware in Pittsburgh, co-founded by Tim Cannon, and figures such as Rich Lee and Jo Zayner are named in that history [1]. DIY brain stimulation began in earnest in late 2011 [6].

The range of activity is broad. The hand-surgery literature covers RFID implants in the hand, which are typically placed outside medical settings [5]. Reviews of the injectable-peptide trend note that unapproved compounds are promoted through social media and sold without prescription for cosmetic and athletic goals [7].

Hand surgeons report infection and tendon attrition from chip implants and note that safety has not been extensively studied [5]. A 2026 review of unregulated biohacking drugs lists product contamination, impurities, inaccurate dosing and unknown long-term effects among concerns for compounds such as BPC-157 and TB-500 [7]. A 2019 Lancet Child and Adolescent Health paper discusses muscles, macronutrients and biohacking as emerging themes in eating disorders among adolescent boys [8].

Biohacking is discussed alongside peptides, bloodwork and recovery protocols as a way to optimise physique and appearance. Hacker News threads from 2011 to 2015 discussed topics such as magnet implants and hand cooling for performance [9][10].
No studies found testing body hacking as a whole. Published work is reviews and perspective pieces on implants, DIY brain stimulation, unregulated peptides and biohacking culture [3][5][6][7][8].

timeline.event: Clynes and Kline publish Cyborgs and Space [1].
Amal Graafstra implants an RFID chip [1].
DIY brain stimulation movement begins in earnest [6].

lore.intro: Body hacking is discussed in forums as a mindset of self-experimentation and in tech communities as implants and gadgets [9][10].

claims.claim: Self-experimentation with tracking and compounds can optimise energy and physique
claims.believers: Practitioners say measuring and iterating on their own data lets them find what works for them.
claims.experts: Reviews note that unapproved biohacking drugs lack established human safety profiles [7].

claims.claim: Implants are a low-risk way to extend the body
claims.believers: Implant enthusiasts describe RFID and magnet chips as everyday tools [1][5].
claims.experts: Hand surgeons report infection and tendon attrition and limited safety study [5].
